title: Off The Map
epigraph: Malachus Archive, municipal record 44-C. Four months before the Registration. Glitch count, that month: nine.
blurb: A grid contractor finds a pipe carrying water a god says does not exist, and a maintenance door that was painted shut sixty years ago. What is behind the door is a street. What is in his own notebook is worse.

image.depicts: Block 44 at street level during a stutter — half-power lighting, doors wedged open the length of the street, the water reclamation building at one end. No figures.
image.spoilerCheck: PASS. Geography and weather only. No Cole, no shaft, no sub-level, nothing underground.
image.hardConstraints: NOBODY IN FRAME. The street is lit at half power and the doors are open, but nothing is wrong in a way that reads as an emergency — this is a working block having an ordinary bad evening.

COLOUR IDENTITY OF THIS PLATE: COLD STREET, WARM DOORWAYS. Two colours doing

{{LOC:BLOCK_44_SURFACE}}
NO FIGURES ANYWHERE IN THIS PLATE. Nobody in the street, nobody in a doorway,
nobody at a window, not a silhouette. The block is occupied and everyone is
inside, and that is what the picture is about.
Evening, at the fourth bell, in the middle of a glitch stutter.
THE STREET LIGHTING IS AT HALF POWER and it is uneven — some fixtures dim, some
out entirely, the light pooling and then failing between them. Do not light
this street evenly.
DOORS ALONG BOTH SIDES ARE WEDGED OPEN and windows are cracked, the whole block
doing the same thing at the same time without anyone having been told to. Warm
interior light leaks out of every one of those gaps, which is the only warm

LEFT HALF: the residential run — heavy blockwork frontages, exposed conduit,
service hatches, the propped doors and their spill of warm light. It must work
alone as a picture of a street where every door is open and nobody is out.
RIGHT HALF: the water reclamation building at the end of the block, squat and
industrial, with the ACCESS SHAFT head behind it — a plain municipal hatch,
closed, unremarkable, not lit and not emphasised.
The roadway runs unbroken across both halves so they read as one view.
Camera low, street level, looking down the length of the block.
Deep navy and near-black structure, cold dim cyan-white from the failing street
fixtures, warm amber leaking from the propped doors. NOT ruined, NOT abandoned,
NOT foggy — just a normal street at reduced power.

title.title: Off The Map
title.epigraph: Malachus Archive, municipal record 44-C. Four months before the Registration. Glitch count, that month: nine.

blocks.v: Part One: The Callout

Cole Porter was a grid contractor. For twenty-two years, when something broke under Haven City that Seraph's repair units couldn't reach or couldn't figure out, the dispatch system sent Cole. Old junctions. Pre-Seraph pipework. The parts of the city that were older than the god that ran it.

He carried municipal certification, a diagnostic lens over his left eye that read grid signatures through walls, and a paper notebook in his chest pocket with twenty-two years of jobs in it, written in pencil.

The younger contractors laughed at the notebook. Everything was supposed to be logged to the grid, and Cole logged to the grid like everyone else. But he wrote it down too, because the grid's records had started coming back wrong. Nine glitches that month. Work orders with addresses he didn't remember. Invoices that changed size overnight. The records belonged to Seraph, and Seraph had been getting things wrong.
Paper didn't glitch. That was the reason for the notebook.

He'd slept badly the night before, which he only mentioned to himself because it was the dream again. He'd been having it on and off for three years. A white ceiling. Someone humming, low and even. A woman's voice, very gentle, saying something he could never hold onto after he woke. It wasn't a nightmare. That was the strange part. He always woke from it calm, and the calm always felt like it belonged to somebody else.
The callout came at the fourth evening bell, in the middle of a stutter, which told him it was bad. Dispatch didn't interrupt a glitch for small things.

image.caption: Twenty-two years of jobs, in pencil, because paper does not glitch.
image.depicts: Cole Porter at the end of a shift, writing the day into the paper notebook. The diagnostic lens over the left eye, the pencil, the kit.
image.spoilerCheck: PASS. Establishes the man and the notebook before anything happens. No door, no pipe, no street below.
image.hardConstraints: This is the plate that establishes Cole AND the notebook. The lens is over the LEFT eye and is INACTIVE here — no amber glow. The pencil is in his hand and the notebook is open.
image.prompt:
{{STYLE}}
PALETTE MODE: PS-2 SUNSET EMBER, read as INDOOR LAMPLIGHT rather than sky.

>>> THIS IS A WARM PLATE, AND IT IS THE LAST ONE FOR A WHILE. <<<
A previous version of this plate was near-black with a single lamp, which put
it in the same register as the four plates that follow it and made the whole
opening of the volume read as one long dark corridor. It should not.
This is a man at the end of an ordinary working day in a room he knows. Light
it like that: AMBER, OCHRE AND WARM CREAM across most of the frame, the lamp
generous rather than mean, the work surface and the open page genuinely bright.
Let the warm light reach the walls instead of dying two feet from the bulb.
MID-KEY, NOT LOW-KEY. Shadow is present and shaped but it is not the subject —
a reader should be able to see the whole room. Deep navy only in the corners.
Everything after this gets colder and darker, and that only lands if this one
is warm.
{{CHAR:COLE}}
ONE FIGURE ONLY. Cole, at the end of a shift. No other person in frame.
THIS PLATE ESTABLISHES TWO THINGS AND THEY ARE EQUALLY IMPORTANT: the man, and
the paper notebook. Compose so that both are unmistakable.
He sits at a plain municipal work surface with his kit set down beside him —
tools, the shoulder lamp, a coil of line, all of it used. He is WRITING IN THE
NOTEBOOK WITH A PENCIL, the book flat and open in front of him, his weight on
one forearm. Pencil, not a stylus, not a pen, not a screen.
The notebook is small, paper, worn soft at the corners, thick with twenty-two
years. Show enough of the open page to read as handwriting without any text
being legible.
THE LENS IS OVER HIS LEFT EYE AND IT IS SWITCHED OFF. No amber cast, no glow, no
projection — this is the one plate where the tool is idle, so that its light
means something in later plates. It is a scuffed, repaired, municipal rig, and
it should look like equipment issued to a tradesman rather than anything
military or elegant.
He is unhurried. Not tired, not troubled, not brooding. A competent man doing
the last small task of a working day.
Medium, slightly high, from across the work surface, so the open notebook is
square to camera and his face is turned down toward it.
Deep navy and near-black room, one warm amber work lamp doing all the lighting
from the left, the open page the brightest surface in the frame. Almost no
saturation anywhere except that amber.

blocks.v: WATER MAIN BREACH. SECTOR 9, BLOCK 44, SUB-LEVEL. PRESSURE LOSS 40%. ASSIGNED: PORTER, C.
He read it twice. He knew Block 44's sub-level. He'd done a valve job down there five or six years ago, and there wasn't enough pipe down there to lose forty percent of anything.

The corridor lights were still at half power when he shouldered his kit. Up and down the street, doors were wedged open and windows were cracked. Nobody had told anyone to do it. The block just did it now, the way you close shutters before a storm. The air had the thin, flat taste it got when the atmospheric processors fell behind. Fourth stutter that week. People barely looked up from their dinners anymore.
The access shaft behind the water reclamation building took his code on the third try. He clipped his lamp to his shoulder and went down the ladder into the dark under Block 44.
His boots hit standing water at the bottom. Two inches and rising.

image.caption: Two inches, and rising.
image.depicts: Cole descending the access ladder into the sub-level, shoulder lamp lit, the hatch a small bright square far above him.
image.spoilerCheck: PASS. He is on the way down. Nothing of the gallery, the pipe or the door is visible yet.
image.hardConstraints: Camera is BELOW him looking up. He is small in the frame and the darkness around him is most of the picture. Standing water at the bottom edge, catching the lamp.
image.prompt:
{{STYLE}}
PALETTE MODE: PS-1 NIGHT NOIR, COLD — but ELECTRIC, not empty.

>>> COLOUR IDENTITY: COLD STEEL, LIT BY THE CITY'S OWN HARDWARE. <<<
The plate before this is warm amber. This one drops the warmth completely, and
that change should be felt on the turn of the page. The shoulder lamp is HARD,
WHITE AND SLIGHTLY BLUE — a working light, not a hearth. No amber, no ochre,
no gold anywhere, including in the water.

BUT THIS IS NOT A BARE CONCRETE HOLE. It is a maintained municipal shaft in a
working city, and it is full of the city's own small electric lights:
  - a CYAN or ELECTRIC-BLUE guidance strip running the full height of the
    shaft beside the ladder, marking the descent, receding to a point
  - small hot GREEN and AMBER status LEDs on junction boxes and cable
    clamps at intervals down the wall, each one a tiny sharp point of colour
  - one MAGENTA or VIOLET indicator on the hatch mechanism above
These are small, saturated and precise, and they give the shaft its depth —
the eye should read the drop by counting lights. They do not illuminate the
blockwork; they are points, not lamps.

HIGH CONTRAST: hard white and small saturated points against near-black. The
plate should read as a lit technical structure at night, NOT as a ruin, a
bunker, or a hole in the ground.
>>> COLOUR IDENTITY: STEEL AND CONCRETE. NO WARMTH ANYWHERE. <<<
The plate before this one is warm amber. This one drops that completely and
the change should be felt on the turn of the page.
The shoulder lamp is HARD, WHITE AND SLIGHTLY BLUE — a working light, not a
hearth. It does not warm the blockwork it hits. No amber, no ochre, no gold
anywhere in this plate, including in the water.
Everything else is cold grey-blue stone, black shaft and one small COLD-WHITE
rectangle of street light far above. Near-monochrome: this is the plate with
the least colour in the volume, and it is the hinge between the warm surface
and everything below.
HIGHEST CONTRAST IN THE VOLUME — hard white against near-black, very little in
between. Where other plates use midtones, this one mostly does not have any.
{{LOC:BLOCK_44_SURFACE}}
{{CHAR:COLE}}
ONE FIGURE. Cole on the ladder, most of the way down. Nobody else.
CAMERA IS AT THE BOTTOM OF THE SHAFT, LOOKING STRAIGHT UP. This is the only
vertical composition in the volume and it should feel like one — a tall narrow
picture of a man coming down into somewhere.
The access shaft is old municipal work: a steel ladder bolted to blockwork,
cable runs and conduit strapped up one side, rust bleeding at the fixings.
Cole is descending, one hand on a rung, kit on his back, THE SHOULDER LAMP LIT
and throwing its cone down past him toward camera so we are looking into it.
He is SMALL in the frame. The dark is the subject and he is the thing inside it.
FAR ABOVE HIM, the open hatch is a small bright rectangle of half-power street
light — the surface, already a long way off. It should read as small enough to
feel like a way out rather than an exit.
At the very bottom edge of frame, STANDING WATER, black and still, holding the
lamp's reflection. Two inches of it. It is the first thing the picture tells
you is wrong.
THE LENS IS NOT ACTIVE YET. No amber glow on his face.
Deep navy blockwork, near-black shaft, one hard cone of warm-white lamp light,
a small cold rectangle of sky-light above, and the black water below. Almost no
colour in the plate at all.

blocks.v: Part Two: Below

The sub-level was a service gallery, pipe and conduit running along both walls. His lamp lit a long cone that ended in black. The lens overlaid the grid map on his left eye, water lines in blue, power in yellow, every piece of the city's body tagged and numbered.
The water was coming from the north end. He waded toward it, and the pressure readout dropped another point while he walked.
He found the breach at the gallery's north wall, and he stood there longer than he should have, because it didn't make sense.

The main had split at a junction collar. That part was ordinary. But the water wasn't coming out of the wall. It was coming out of a pipe that ran *through* the wall, a heavy feeder line entering the gallery from the north, and when Cole put his lens on it, the lens drew nothing. No blue line. No tag. No number. The map showed the gallery ending at solid foundation three meters ahead of him.

image.shotType: Wide, the gallery, lamp cone into black
image.caption: A cone of light that ended in nothing, and every pipe in it with a number.
image.depicts: The sub-level service gallery — pipe and conduit on both walls, standing water underfoot, Cole small in the middle with the grid overlay active.
image.spoilerCheck: PASS. Establishes the gallery and the grid overlay. The unmarked pipe and the door are further north and not yet in shot.
image.hardConstraints: THE OVERLAY IS ESTABLISHED HERE: every pipe carries a fine electric-blue wireframe line and a tag. That is what makes its absence in the next plate legible. Water lines blue, power lines yellow.
image.prompt:
{{STYLE}}
PALETTE MODE: PS-1 NIGHT NOIR, ELECTRIC BLUE OVERLAY PLUS THE ROOM'S OWN LIGHTS.

>>> COLOUR IDENTITY: THE RICHEST, MOST ELECTRIC PLATE UNDERGROUND. <<<
This plate and the one two after it share a room, so they must not share a
look. THIS one is the full, lit, working gallery. The next one is austere and
nearly colourless. Push this one the other way.

THE LENS OVERLAY is electric blue, spread across both walls, doubled in the
water. It is the dominant colour.

AND THE GALLERY HAS ITS OWN LIGHTS, WHICH ARE NOT THE OVERLAY. This is
maintained municipal infrastructure in a working city, not an abandoned sewer:
  - CYAN-WHITE strip lighting along the ceiling line, some sections dead, the
    live ones marking the gallery's length
  - hot GREEN and AMBER status points on valve assemblies and junction boxes
  - one MAGENTA-VIOLET glow further down the gallery from a powered cabinet,
    the only warm-cool clash in the frame, throwing colour across the water
All of it reflects in the standing water, so the floor carries the whole
palette a second time, broken.

The shoulder lamp stays WARM-WHITE and TIGHT — a small cone on Cole only. Warm
tool, cold world.

A reader should register this plate as ELECTRIC AND ALIVE, the shaft before it
as COLD, and the pipe plate after it as ALMOST NOTHING.
>>> COLOUR IDENTITY: THIS IS THE BLUE PLATE. <<<
The overlay is not an accent here, it is the colour story. Electric blue is the
first thing a reader sees, it is spread across the whole width of the picture
on both walls, and it is reflected in the water so it runs twice.
The shoulder lamp stays WARM-WHITE but keep it SMALL and CONTAINED — a tight
cone around Cole only. It must not compete with the blue or spread warmth
across the gallery. Warm tool, cold data, and the data is winning this frame.
Everything not blue and not in the lamp cone is deep cold navy going to black.
A reader flipping past should register this plate as BLUE, the plate before it
as GREY, and the plate after it as ALMOST NOTHING.
{{LOC:SUB_LEVEL_GALLERY}}
{{CHAR:COLE}}
ONE FIGURE, AND HE IS SMALL. Cole stands about THIRTY FEET from camera, deep
enough that he is roughly a fifth of the frame height and reads as a figure in
a space rather than as a portrait. A previous attempt put him close and large,
filling the lower frame, which turns the gallery into a backdrop. THE GALLERY
IS THE SUBJECT and he is the thing that gives it scale.
THIS PLATE'S JOB IS TO ESTABLISH THE GRID OVERLAY SO THAT ITS ABSENCE MEANS
SOMETHING TWO PLATES LATER.

>>> THE OVERLAY IS NOT PHYSICALLY IN THE ROOM. <<<
This is the single most important thing about this plate. The overlay is a
PROJECTION THAT EXISTS ONLY INSIDE COLE'S LENS — data drawn over the world,
the way a heads-up display sits over what you are looking at. It is made of
light and it is weightless.
IT IS EXPLICITLY NOT: painted markings, stencilled numbers, enamel or metal
placards, bolted-on signs, printed labels, tape, hazard plates, or anything
else fixed to a pipe. NOTHING IN THIS GALLERY IS LABELLED. Somebody walking
through here without the lens would see bare unmarked pipe.
A previous attempt hung orange sign plates off every pipe. That version is
wrong twice over: the plate carries lettering, and it destroys the next
plate, where a pipe the overlay refuses to acknowledge has to read as the map
denying the pipe exists — not as a sign nobody got round to screwing on.

SO DRAW IT LIKE THIS:
- EVERY pipe and conduit carries a fine ELECTRIC-BLUE WIREFRAME line running
  along its length, floating a hair off the surface, following the pipe's
  curve like a contour rather than sitting on it like paint. Water lines
  blue, power lines a cold yellow.
- At each junction, a small SELF-LUMINOUS tick or bracket of the same blue,
  thin and machine-drawn and clearly weightless.
- NO NUMBERS, NO LETTERS, NO CHARACTERS OF ANY KIND ANYWHERE IN THIS PLATE.
  Not on the overlay, not on the walls, not on a hatch. The tags are marks,
  not writing — an unreadable technical notation a viewer takes in at a
  glance without being able to read one character of it.
- The overlay does not light the gallery. It casts nothing on the walls and
  does not warm the water. Only the shoulder lamp lights anything.
The gallery runs away from camera, pipe and conduit banked along both walls,
low ceiling, pre-Seraph blockwork that is heavier and cruder than anything on
the surface.
STANDING WATER covers the floor and reflects the overlay, so the blue lines run
twice — once on the pipes and once, broken, underneath them.
Cole is thirty feet in, waist-lit by his own shoulder lamp, walking away from
camera. THE LENS IS ACTIVE and throws its warm amber-gold cast on the LEFT
side of his face only — warm tool, cold data, never the same colour.
THE LAMP CONE ENDS IN BLACK. The far end of the gallery is not dark, it is
absent — the light simply stops and there is nothing beyond it.
Wide, low, near the water's surface so the reflections carry.
Near-black and deep navy, one warm-white lamp cone, and the electric blue of the
overlay as the only saturated colour anywhere in the frame.

blocks.v: The pipe came out of a wall the map said was solid, carrying water the grid said didn't exist.
He wiped the lens and rebooted it. While it came back up he kept his bare eye on the pipe.
The map redrew. Solid wall. No pipe.

Cole knew every kind of map error there was. Stale surveys. Scrambled tags. Pre-Seraph pipe that had never been logged right. This wasn't any of them. Unlogged pipe showed up as a gray hash, the grid's way of saying it saw something it couldn't name. This pipe wasn't unnamed. It was missing. The map wasn't saying *I can't read that*. The map was saying *there is nothing there*, and it was saying it with a god's full confidence.

He clamped the breach. It took forty minutes and the water numbed his hands, and the pressure gauge told him something he didn't like the whole time: the feeder line beyond the wall was drawing steady, metered flow. Not a leak. A supply. Somebody's supply.
When the clamp held, he walked the wall.

image.shotType: Medium, the north wall, the pipe
image.caption: The map was not saying it could not read that. It was saying there was nothing there.
image.depicts: The unmarked feeder pipe coming through the north wall — every other pipe in frame tagged in blue, this one carrying no line, no tag and no number at all.
image.spoilerCheck: PASS. The pipe only. The maintenance door is four meters east and is NOT in this frame.
image.hardConstraints: THE KEY IMAGE OF THE VOLUME. Every pipe in frame is tagged EXCEPT the heavy feeder line, which has nothing on it. The absence must be immediately obvious. The wall it comes through is drawn as unbroken foundation.
image.prompt:
{{STYLE}}
PALETTE MODE: PS-1 NIGHT NOIR at its DARKEST AND MOST COMPRESSED.

>>> COLOUR IDENTITY: NEARLY NO COLOUR AT ALL. <<<
The plate before this one is saturated blue across the full frame. This one
pulls almost all of that away and works in VALUE instead of hue, because the
subject is an absence and a loud picture cannot show an absence.
Only a FEW blue-tagged runs are in frame and they sit at the edges, dimmer and
sparser than in the previous plate. The centre of the picture, where the bare
feeder pipe is, has NO blue in it at all.
The rest is near-black wet stone with a narrow range of cold greys — a quiet,
close, almost monochrome plate. It should feel like the volume holding its
breath, and it is the darkest picture in the book.
{{LOC:SUB_LEVEL_GALLERY}}
NO FIGURES, or at most Cole's gloved hand and forearm entering the frame at the
edge. The pipe is the subject and nothing competes with it.
THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT PLATE IN THE VOLUME AND IT IS ONE IDEA:
EVERY PIPE IN THIS FRAME IS TAGGED. ONE PIPE IS NOT.

>>> THE TAGS ARE LENS PROJECTION, NOT SIGNAGE. <<< Same rule as the plate two
back, and it is what makes this image mean anything. The blue lines and ticks
are weightless data drawn over the world by the lens. They are NOT painted
markings, stencils, bolted placards or printed labels, and NOTHING in this
gallery is physically labelled. If the tags read as signs, the bare pipe just
looks unlabelled — the point is that the map denies the pipe is there at all.
NO NUMBERS AND NO LETTERS ANYWHERE IN THIS PLATE. The notation is marks only.
- The ordinary municipal runs along the walls all carry the fine electric-blue
  wireframe line and the junction ticks, exactly as established two plates back.
- The HEAVY FEEDER PIPE entering through the north wall carries NOTHING. No
  line. No tag. No number. No hash, no dashes, no grey outline, no error mark,
  no question mark, no glitch artefact. The overlay does not fail on it — the
  overlay simply does not acknowledge it. It is the only bare object in a room
  where everything else has been labelled.
- Do not draw anything to indicate the discrepancy. No highlight, no red, no
  arrow, no UI warning. The picture must let the viewer notice it.
The pipe is old, heavy, industrial, sweating, and it emerges from what reads as
UNBROKEN FOUNDATION STONE — no frame, no collar, no opening around it. It comes
out of solid wall.
A split at a junction collar nearby is throwing water; the standing water is
deeper here and moving.
MEDIUM, level, square to the north wall so the contrast between the tagged runs
and the bare pipe is a straight visual comparison across the frame.
Near-black and deep navy stone, wet highlights, electric blue notation on
everything but the one pipe. The bare pipe is the darkest, plainest, most
ordinary object in the picture, and that is what makes it wrong.

blocks.v: The lens said foundation stone. His hands found the seam anyway, four meters east of the pipe, under sixty years of paint and grime. The outline of a maintenance door, sealed so long ago the hinges had been painted into the wall.
He put his palm flat against the steel. It was warm.

He stood there with his hand on the warm door and thought about the dream. He didn't know why. The white ceiling, the humming, the voice. It came up out of nowhere, the way a smell brings something back, and it was gone again just as fast.

He took the pry bar off his kit. Opening sealed doors wasn't his job, and he was three years from a pension, and he did it anyway, and if you'd asked him why, the honest answer was that the map had lied to him and he wanted to know what it was lying about.
The door gave on the third pull.

image.caption: Sixty years of paint, and under it a door, and the door was warm.
image.depicts: Cole's bare palm flat against the painted-over outline of a sealed maintenance door, the seam visible under decades of paint.
image.spoilerCheck: PASS. The door is still shut. Nothing behind it is visible or implied by light.
image.hardConstraints: The door is SHUT and there is NO light leaking around it. The seam is visible only as a shape under paint. His hand is BARE — the glove is off, because he is feeling for warmth.
image.prompt:
{{STYLE}}
PALETTE MODE: PS-1 NIGHT NOIR, SHIFTED GREEN. This plate is not navy.

>>> COLOUR IDENTITY: SIXTY YEARS OF INSTITUTIONAL PAINT. <<<
The door has been painted over so many times the colour has become the subject.
A pale, chalky, INSTITUTIONAL GREEN — municipal, old, slightly sickly, the
green of a corridor nobody has looked at since it was built — going grey and
blistered where damp has got under it. THAT GREEN FILLS MOST OF THE FRAME and
it should look wrong beside the plates around it.

Cole's BARE SKIN is the only warm thing in the picture. His hand MUST be bare —
the glove is off, held in his other hand or pushed into a pocket. A version of
this plate came back with a gloved hand, which loses the whole gesture: he took
the glove off because he is feeling for warmth through the paint.

ONE COLD ELECTRIC ACCENT, SMALL AND OFF TO THE SIDE: a cyan or violet status
light on a powered junction box a few feet away, just enough to say the city is
still running here and this door is the only dead thing in the frame. It must
not light the hand and must not compete with the green.

NO ELECTRIC BLUE OVERLAY ANYWHERE IN THIS PLATE. The lens is drawing nothing
here, which is exactly why he is using his hand instead.
>>> COLOUR IDENTITY: SIXTY YEARS OF INSTITUTIONAL PAINT. <<<
The door has been painted over so many times the colour has become the subject.
It is a pale, chalky, INSTITUTIONAL GREEN — municipal, old, slightly sickly,
the green of a corridor nobody has looked at since it was built — going grey
and blistered where damp has got under it.
THAT GREEN FILLS MOST OF THE FRAME and it should look wrong next to the plates
around it, because that is the point: the wall is the only thing down here
that was made by people who meant it to be seen.
Cole's BARE SKIN is the only warm thing in the picture — a hand against all
that cold green, and the contrast is what makes the gesture read.
No electric blue in this plate. The lens is not drawing anything here, which
is why he has taken the glove off and is using his hand instead.
{{LOC:SUB_LEVEL_GALLERY}}
{{CHAR:COLE}}
TIGHT. A hand, a wall, and part of a face. This is the closest plate in the
volume and it should feel like the camera has moved in.
Cole's BARE PALM is flat against the wall — the glove is off and pushed into a
pocket or held in the other hand, because he has taken it off deliberately to
feel something.
Under his hand, the OUTLINE OF A MAINTENANCE DOOR is just visible: a rectangular
seam buried under sixty years of municipal paint, the hinges painted over so
completely they are lumps rather than hardware. Layered paint, chipped in
places, grime in the seam. The door is a SHAPE, not an object — you can see
where it is, not what it is.
THE DOOR IS SHUT AND THERE IS NO LIGHT AROUND IT. No glow at the seam, no
leak, no warm crack, nothing behind it made visible. The warmth is something he
feels, and the picture must not cheat by showing it.
His face is at the edge of frame, in profile, turned slightly away — he is not
looking at his hand, he is listening to it. THE LENS IS ACTIVE, throwing its
warm amber-gold cast on the LEFT side of his face, and the overlay is
drawing nothing here: the wall in front of him carries no notation at all.
The shoulder lamp rakes ACROSS the wall from one side rather than facing it, so
the seam and the paint texture are picked out by grazing light.
Very tight, level, close enough that the hand fills a third of the frame.
Near-black, deep navy, dead municipal green-grey paint, one hard raking
warm-white light, and the small amber glow at the edge of his face.

blocks.v: Part Three: The Block That Wasn't

Light. That was the first thing. He'd braced for a dead space, an old cistern, a void. Instead there were strings of small white lamps running away from him down a corridor, wired clean, spliced by somebody who knew what they were doing. The corridor opened out thirty meters on, and Cole stopped in the mouth of it and looked at a street.

A street. Underground, low-ceilinged, but a street. Some old sub-level block from before a rebuild nobody remembered, and people lived in it. Laundry hung on lines between the support columns. There was a garden of pale vegetables under grow lamps, planted in beds built out of paving stones. His water, the city's water, ran into a cistern with a valve rig on it that was better work than half the municipal jobs he'd seen. Twenty or thirty small dwellings with curtains for doors. Somewhere, someone was cooking onions.

A dozen people stood in the street looking at him. Human and Valari both, and one Synthetic by the cistern with a wrench in its hand. Nobody ran. Nobody shouted. A woman with a basket of vegetables stopped where she was and watched him, and a child's chalk drawing looped across the paving stones between them, and the whole place just waited, the way people wait when a stranger walks in but not the first stranger.

image.shotType: Wide, the mouth of the corridor
image.caption: He had braced for a void. There was laundry.

image.hardConstraints: THIS IS THE WARMEST PLATE IN THE VOLUME and the palette breaks here after five dark ones. It must read as a HOME — maintained, planted, lit, lived in. Not a slum, not a hideout, not a ruin.
image.prompt:
{{STYLE}}
PALETTE MODE: PS-2 SUNSET EMBER, read as lamplight rather than sky. This is the
warm plate and it is a deliberate break from everything before it.
{{LOC:THE_LOST_BLOCK}}
{{CHAR:COLE}}
Cole is in the FOREGROUND at the mouth of the corridor, small, seen from behind
in near-silhouette, stopped. Residents are present in the middle distance but
UNRESOLVED — figures going about an evening, no faces, nobody addressed. The
place is the subject.
AFTER FIVE DARK PLATES THIS ONE OPENS UP. Depth, warmth and detail everywhere.
It should feel like relief before it feels like anything else.
An entire underground street, low-ceilinged, running away from us between heavy
support columns.
- STRINGS OF SMALL WHITE LAMPS run the length of it, wired clean and spliced
  well. They are the main light and they are strung, not installed.
- LAUNDRY hangs on lines between the columns, catching the lamplight.
- A GARDEN of pale vegetables sits under GROW LAMPS in beds built out of lifted
  paving stones — the one cold-tinted light in a warm plate.
- The CISTERN with its valve rig, visibly good work, better than municipal.
- Twenty or thirty small DWELLINGS with CURTAINS for doors, each with its own
  light behind the curtain.
- Cooking smoke or steam somewhere in the middle distance.
NOTHING HERE IS RUINED, IMPROVISED-LOOKING OR DESPERATE. Everything is
maintained. Somebody sweeps this street.
Wide, level, from the corridor mouth at standing height, so the street runs away
from us with the ceiling low overhead — enclosed, but not oppressive.
Warm amber and soft white from the strung lamps, cool green-white from the grow
lamps as the single cold accent, deep navy structure holding it all in. This is
the only plate in the first two-thirds of the volume with a warm dominant.

blocks.v: That was what got under his skin. He wasn't the first.

A man came toward him. There was nothing unusual about him. Cole would have sworn to that in the moment. It was only afterward, trying to describe him, that he found he couldn't say if the man was tall or short, or old or young, or what his face had looked like at all.
"You're the water man," the man said.
"There's a breach on the main side. Your feeder line was pulling the block's pressure down. Somebody was going to come looking."
"And here you are. Did you fix it?"
"It's clamped. It'll hold." Cole looked past him down the street. "What is this place?"

"It's a block the city lost track of." The man said it the way you'd give directions. "It fell off the map a long time ago. That happens more than you'd think, and it happens more now than it used to. Blocks. Records. Machines." He paused. "People. And when something falls off the map, it needs somewhere to go. This is somewhere."
"Nothing falls off the map," Cole said. "The map is Seraph."
"The map is Seraph's memory. You work the grid. Tell me how Seraph's memory has been running lately."
Cole didn't answer. Nine glitches that month. Work orders that changed overnight. A pipe the grid swore wasn't there, warm water moving through it.

image.shotType: Medium wide, the street, facing him
image.caption: Nobody ran. That was the part that got under his skin.
image.depicts: A dozen residents standing in the street looking back at Cole — Human and Valari, one Synthetic with a wrench by the cistern, a chalk drawing on the stones between them.
image.spoilerCheck: PASS. They are looking, not acting. The man with the book has not yet come forward.
image.hardConstraints: NOBODY IS ALARMED, HOSTILE OR FLEEING. They are waiting, and the waiting reads as practised — he is not the first stranger. The chalk drawing must be clearly a child's and clearly on the paving between him and them.
image.prompt:
{{STYLE}}
PALETTE MODE: PS-2 SUNSET EMBER, lamplight register, matching the previous plate.
{{LOC:THE_LOST_BLOCK}}
About TWELVE RESIDENTS, standing in the street, facing camera. Human and Valari
both. ONE SYNTHETIC stands by the cistern with a WRENCH in its hand, stopped
mid-job.
THE ENTIRE POINT OF THIS PLATE IS WHAT IS NOT HAPPENING.
- NOBODY IS RUNNING. Nobody is shouting, pointing, backing away, reaching for
  anything or shielding a child.
- NOBODY IS THREATENING HIM EITHER. No massing, no advancing, no weapons, no
  hard stares.
- They have simply STOPPED AND TURNED, and they are waiting. The waiting is
  calm and faintly practised, the way people wait when a stranger walks in but
  not the FIRST stranger. That practised quality is the horror of the plate and
  it lives entirely in the body language.
A WOMAN WITH A BASKET OF VEGETABLES has stopped exactly where she was, basket
still on her hip, watching him. She is the closest figure and the clearest read.
The Valari present have circuits in the ordinary soft-blue-to-dusty-magenta-violet
range, low and unsaturated, unremarkable — these are people at home, not a
faction.
ACROSS THE PAVING BETWEEN CAMERA AND THE GROUP, a CHILD'S CHALK DRAWING loops
over the stones — obviously a child's, obviously recent, and directly in the
space between him and them. It is the softest thing in the picture and it is
lying in the gap.
Medium wide, level, from Cole's eyeline, so the viewer is standing where he is.
Cole himself is NOT in frame.
Warm amber strung lamps, the cool green-white grow lamps behind, chalk white and
pale pastel on grey paving. Faces warmly lit and completely unfrightened.

blocks.v: "Go home, water man," the man said. "Bill your hours to the glitch. Don't report the water. Not to protect us. Because there's nowhere to report it to. The report goes into the grid, and the grid can't hold a file about a place it says doesn't exist. It'll be gone by morning and you'll look like a man who files reports about nothing."
He stepped closer. Cole held his ground, and it took more than it should have.
"And forget the door," the man said. "That part's easier than you'd think."
Then he asked, politely, like a clerk, "What's your name?"
"Cole Porter."

The man took a small book out of his coat. A paper book, worn soft at the corners, thick with use. He wrote in it with a pencil stub and put it away, and Cole stood in a street that didn't exist, watching a stranger write his name in a notebook just like his own, and felt the fear arrive late, the way it does when you've already stepped on the loose board.
"Go on home," the man said. "You did good work tonight."

image.caption: A stranger, writing his name in a notebook just like his own.
image.depicts: The man with the book writing Cole Porter's name with a pencil stub, the small worn paper book open in his hands.
image.spoilerCheck: PASS. Shows the name being taken. Nothing of the white room, Sister Silence or the three-year-old entry.
image.hardConstraints: THE BOOK IS THE SUBJECT AND THE FACE IS NOT. The man must be impossible to describe afterward — average everything, no strong feature, never masked or blurred. His book and Cole's notebook must be visibly the same KIND of object.
image.prompt:
{{STYLE}}
PALETTE MODE: PS-2 SUNSET EMBER, lamplight register, but pulled DOWN — this is

>>> BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE: HIS FACE IS UNCOVERED AND FULLY LIT. <<<
An attempt at this plate came back with him in a deep hood with his face in
shadow. That is the exact opposite of this character and it fails the plate.
NO HOOD UP. NO MASK. NO SCARF. NO SHADOW ACROSS THE FACE. NO BLUR. NO CROP
THAT HIDES HIM. NO TURNING AWAY FROM CAMERA.
His whole face is visible, evenly lit, and drawn in full detail — and it is
still a face you could not describe an hour later, because there is nothing
remarkable in it. That is the trick: he is unmemorable because he is ORDINARY,
never because he is concealed. A hidden face is the most memorable thing in a
picture, which is why hiding him breaks the character completely.

>>> AND: NOT ONE READABLE LETTER ANYWHERE IN THIS PLATE. <<<
An attempt came back with the name written out in clear script. The name being
taken is the POINT of the scene and it must still be ILLEGIBLE — pencil marks
with the rhythm and slope of handwriting and no formed word in them. Do not
write "Cole Porter". Do not write anything. The reader is told what is being
written; the picture only shows that writing is happening.
the darkest of the three lost-block plates.
{{LOC:THE_LOST_BLOCK}}
{{CHAR:THE_CARTOGRAPHER}}
{{CHAR:COLE}}
TWO FIGURES, close. The man writing; Cole facing him.
THE BOOK IS THE SUBJECT OF THIS PICTURE AND THE FACE IS NOT. Compose so the
open book and the pencil stub are the sharpest, best-lit, most central things
in the frame.
The man holds a SMALL PAPER BOOK open on his palm, worn soft at the corners and
thick with use, and is writing in it with a PENCIL STUB. The gesture is
unhurried and clerical — this is a man doing routine paperwork, not performing
a threat. Show handwriting on the page without a single word being legible.
HIS FACE IS THE HARD PART. It must be present, lit enough to see, and STILL
impossible to fix in memory. Average height, average build, plain coat in a
colour that is not quite a colour. No scar, no strong jaw, no memorable nose,
no augmentation, no expression worth naming. Keep him slightly turned and
slightly soft so the face never fully resolves.
DO NOT MASK HIM, HOOD HIM, SHADOW HIM OUT OR BLUR HIM. An obscured face is
memorable, and memorable is the exact opposite of this character. He must be
plainly visible and still forgettable.
COLE'S OWN NOTEBOOK IS VISIBLE IN HIS CHEST POCKET IN THIS FRAME, and it is
manifestly the same KIND of object as the book being written in — same size,
same wear, same soft corners. That rhyme is the point of the plate.
Cole is close, his body squared and holding still with visible effort.
Tight two-shot, level, slightly favouring the book — near enough that both
books are in the frame and the street behind is only warm blur.
Amber lamplight from one side, deep navy behind, the open page the brightest
surface in the picture and the graphite mark the darkest.

blocks.v: Part Four: The White Room

Cole came up the ladder at the second morning bell. The stutter had passed. The lights were full, the air tasted like air, and the city was doing what it always did after a glitch, which was pretend nothing had happened.
He filed the repair from the corner terminal. The grid took the clamp job, logged his hours, and added a line to the work order:
CAUSE: PRESSURE ANOMALY, SOURCE UNRESOLVED. SUB-LEVEL SURVEY: NO ADDITIONAL STRUCTURES PRESENT.

He read that line twice. Somewhere under his boots there was a street with laundry on lines and a chalk drawing and thirty people cooking onions, and the memory of the whole world said: nothing there.
He walked home. He sat down at his kitchen table in the gray early light and took out the notebook to write it down, because the grid couldn't hold this, and his book could.
The pencil was in his hand when he noticed a dog-eared page further back. He didn't dog-ear pages.
He turned to it. Three years old, between a filter job and a conduit rebuild. His own handwriting. His own pencil.
*Block 44 sub-level. Door in the north wall past the junction. Warm. There's a street behind it. People. Man with a book took my name. Said forget the door.*
And under that, underlined twice, pressed hard enough to nearly tear the paper:

image.caption: NO ADDITIONAL STRUCTURES PRESENT.
image.depicts: Cole at a corner terminal in an ordinary morning street, having just filed the repair, reading the line the grid added to his work order.
image.spoilerCheck: PASS. Surface, daylight, aftermath. Nothing of the notebook discovery or the white room.
image.hardConstraints: THE CITY IS COMPLETELY NORMAL. Full light, ordinary traffic of people, nothing wrong anywhere — the contrast with the previous three plates is the whole point. No text on the terminal is legible.
image.prompt:
{{STYLE}}
PALETTE MODE: PS-3 SKYLINE DAY.
{{CHAR:COLE}}
ONE FIGURE SHARP: Cole at a public corner terminal. Ordinary passers-by around
him, unremarkable and out of focus.
THE JOB OF THIS PLATE IS THAT NOTHING IS WRONG. After the sub-level and the
lost block, the city is simply having a normal morning: full light, clean air,
people going to work, a delivery cart, somebody eating. Not one thing in the
frame is sinister. That is what makes it land.
Cole stands at the terminal with one hand still resting on it, having just
filed. He has stopped moving. His head is level and he is READING something,
and his stillness is the only thing in the picture that does not fit the
morning around him.
The terminal is plain municipal hardware on a corner post. ITS SCREEN IS
VISIBLE BUT NO TEXT ON IT IS LEGIBLE — lines of type that read as a record
without being readable. Do not write words on the screen.
THE LENS OVER HIS LEFT EYE IS OFF. Morning light on his face, no amber cast, and
he looks like any tradesman who has been up all night — which he is.
He is still wet to the knee. His boots and the lower legs of his coat are
soaked and dark, and that detail is the only evidence in the plate that the
night happened at all.
Medium, level, from across the pavement, with the ordinary street traffic
passing between camera and him so he is glimpsed rather than presented.
Pale cyan sky, cream and sand stone, long clean morning light. Fully lit, open,
unremarkable. The most ordinary plate in the volume, on purpose.

blocks.v: *DON'T FORGET THE DOOR.*
He had no memory of writing it. He read it four times and nothing came. Not the door, not the street, not the man. Three years gone, clean.
And then something did come, but it wasn't the door.
The white ceiling.
It arrived all at once, the way the dream never did, whole and sharp, and for the first time in three years he could hold onto it. He wasn't dreaming it. He was remembering it.

A room with white tile walls and a white ceiling and light that came from everywhere, so there were no shadows in it at all. He was lying on a table that was comfortable, which was somehow the worst detail, that they had made it comfortable. Figures stood along the wall in desert-gray, four of them, hoods up, and they moved together, when one shifted its weight the others shifted, like they were all hearing the same slow song. One of them was humming. The sound never changed and never stopped.

And a woman was leaning over him. Small. Valari. Old in a way that didn't show in her skin, only in how still she was. Her circuits were the faintest silver, barely lit, like frost. She had her palm flat on his forehead, and her hand was cool and dry, and she was looking at him with what he could only ever describe afterward as kindness, real kindness, the kind you couldn't fake, and that was the most frightening thing he had ever seen.

image.caption: His own handwriting, three years old, telling him something he had never once remembered.
image.depicts: The notebook open on a kitchen table in grey morning light, showing a dog-eared page of three-year-old handwriting with a line underlined twice.
image.spoilerCheck: PASS. The page and the table. No figure, no white room, no Sister Silence.
image.hardConstraints: NO PEOPLE IN FRAME, at most a hand at the edge. The underlined line must be visibly pressed hard enough to have nearly torn the paper. No handwriting anywhere in the plate is legible as actual words.
image.prompt:
{{STYLE}}
PALETTE MODE: PS-3 SKYLINE DAY, at its coldest and flattest — early grey light

>>> BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE: NOT ONE READABLE WORD IN THIS PLATE. <<<
An attempt at this plate came back as a fully written page — a legible diary
entry, headings, labels, a drawn map, notes in the margin. All of it wrong.
THE PAGE CARRIES NO WORDS, NO HEADINGS, NO LABELS, NO DATES, NO NUMBERS AND NO
DIAGRAMS. What it carries is the LOOK of handwriting: lines of pencil marks
with the slope, rhythm, spacing and ragged right edge of a real page of notes,
and not one of those marks resolves into a letter.
This is not a detail. The prose tells the reader what the page says, and the
moment the picture says it too, the plate is doing the writing's job badly
instead of doing its own job well.
The ONE thing that must read clearly is the DOUBLE UNDERLINE and the pressure
ridge under it — pressed hard enough to have nearly torn the paper. That mark
is the whole plate. Everything else on the page is texture.
through a kitchen window, before the sun is properly up.
NO FIGURES IN THIS PLATE. At most one hand resting at the very edge of frame.
This is a still life and the object is doing all the work.
A PLAIN KITCHEN TABLE, worn, with the paper NOTEBOOK OPEN on it and a PENCIL
lying where it was put down. A cup of coffee, going cold, off to one side.
Nothing else on the table.
THE PAGE IS THE SUBJECT. It is a DOG-EARED page from three years back, and the
dog-ear is clearly visible as a folded corner — the one deliberate mark on an
otherwise plain book.
On the page, handwriting in PENCIL, filling several lines, and beneath it a
single line UNDERLINED TWICE and pressed so hard the pencil has almost torn
through the paper. The double underline and the pressure ridge must both be
visible — the paper is dented, the graphite is heavy, one stroke has broken the
surface.
NO WORD ANYWHERE IN THIS PLATE IS LEGIBLE. It must read unmistakably as
handwriting, with the shape and rhythm of a note, without a single readable
word. The difference between the ordinary lines and the underlined one is
carried by WEIGHT and PRESSURE, not by content.
Straight OVERHEAD, square to the table, so the page is flat to camera and the
whole spread of the book is in frame.
Cold grey-blue window light from one side, raking just enough to catch the
pressure ridge in the paper and the tooth of the page. Cream paper, graphite
grey, worn brown table, one dull ceramic cup. Almost no colour and no warmth
anywhere in the plate.

blocks.v: "You've been carrying something heavy," she said. Her voice was soft and even. The humming went on underneath it. "You don't have to. That's what people never learn on their own. You don't have to carry it."
He had tried to speak. He remembered that now. He had tried to tell her he wanted to keep it, whatever it was, that it was his.

"I know," she said, like he'd managed to say it. "They always want to keep it. That's the suffering talking." Her palm pressed slightly, no weight at all. "Hold still. This won't hurt. It has never once hurt."
Then the white ceiling, and the humming, and nothing.
Cole sat at his kitchen table with his heart going hard and the notebook open in front of him, and he did the thing he had trusted for twenty-two years. He went to the paper.

The drawer in the hall cabinet held every document he'd ever been handed, because Cole Porter kept paper the way other men kept money. He went through it with cold hands and found it in ten minutes, a single municipal slip he had filed and never once thought about, dated three years back, four days after the notebook entry.
WELLNESS DISCHARGE. PORTER, C. VOLUNTARY RESTORATIVE STAY, 3 DAYS. SPONSOR: SECTOR REFERRAL. CONDITION ON RELEASE: RESTED.

He had a memory of that stay, if he went looking for it. Thin, smooth, no details, like a summary somebody else had written. Work exhaustion. Three days of rest. He'd told the story maybe twice in three years and never questioned it, because who questions a boring story?
Voluntary. Sector referral. He read the slip until the words stopped meaning anything.

image.caption: She was kind to him. That was the most frightening thing he had ever seen.
image.depicts: The white room, remembered whole: Cole on the comfortable table, four gray-hooded figures along the wall, Sister Silence leaning over him with her palm flat on his forehead.
image.spoilerCheck: PASS in place. This is the revelation the volume has been built toward and it belongs here. It shows the memory, not the moment of taking.
image.hardConstraints: THE ROOM HAS NO SHADOWS ANYWHERE — none under the table, none under a chin, none behind a figure. Her expression is GENUINE KINDNESS, never sinister. No restraints, no instruments, no gore. The four hooded figures move as one and none of them is doing anything.
image.prompt:
{{STYLE}}
PALETTE MODE: NONE. THIS PLATE DELIBERATELY BREAKS THE VOLUME'S PALETTE SYSTEM.

>>> THE SUBJECT OF THIS PLATE, BEFORE ANY OTHER INSTRUCTION: <<<
>>> A MAN IS LYING ON HIS BACK ON A TABLE AND A WOMAN HAS HER PALM ON HIS <<<
>>> FOREHEAD. THAT IS THE PICTURE. EVERYTHING ELSE IS THE ROOM. <<<

An attempt at this plate came back as a group of people standing in a circle
around a shrouded body, with Cole on his feet at the edge of frame. Every part
of that is wrong, so it is worth being blunt:
  - COLE IS THE MAN ON THE TABLE. He is not standing, not at the edge, not
    watching. He is lying on his back, face up, and he is the only person
    horizontal in the picture.
  - HE IS AWAKE, DRESSED AND UNHARMED. Eyes open, calm, breathing, in his own
    work clothes. He is NOT wrapped, NOT shrouded, NOT covered by a sheet, NOT
    unconscious and NOT dead. This is not a body and this is not a funeral.
  - A WOMAN'S PALM IS FLAT ON HIS FOREHEAD and that contact is the centre of
    the composition. If a viewer cannot see the hand touching him, the plate
    has failed.

>>> THE CAST IS EXACTLY SIX FIGURES AND NOT ONE MORE. <<<
Cole on the table. Sister Silence at his head. Four Sandmen along the wall,
identical to each other. THAT IS ALL.
NOBODY ELSE IS IN THIS ROOM: no other Valari, no synthetic or android, no
child, no bystander, no second robed figure, no attendant, nobody in the
doorway. Do not add anyone to fill the space — the emptiness of the room is
part of what makes it frightening.
It is white, near-white and desert-gray, and it should look like it does not
belong in the same book as the plates around it. Do not warm it, do not tint it,
do not give it a colour grade.
{{LOC:WHITE_ROOM}}
{{CHAR:COLE}}
{{CHAR:SISTER_SILENCE}}
{{CHAR:SANDMAN}}
SIX FIGURES: Cole on the table, Sister Silence leaning over him, and FOUR
gray-hooded Sandmen standing along the wall.
THE DEFINING INSTRUCTION: THERE ARE NO SHADOWS IN THIS ROOM. Light arrives from
every direction at once. Nothing casts anything — not the table, not a chin,
not a hooded figure, not a hand. No falloff into any corner, no soft gradient on
any wall, no ambient occlusion where surfaces meet. The room should look subtly
impossible and the viewer should not immediately be able to say why.
Cole lies on a table at the centre. THE TABLE IS COMFORTABLE — padded, clean,
considerate, built for somebody's ease. NO RESTRAINTS. No straps, no clamps, no
instruments, no trays, no medical clutter, no wires, no blood, nothing
frightening in any prop. He is calm and his eyes are open.
SISTER SILENCE leans over him, small beside the table, with her PALM FLAT ON
HIS FOREHEAD. The hand is relaxed and weightless. Her circuits are the
FAINTEST SILVER, barely lit, like frost, and visible only as fine tracery at
the hand and jaw — not blue, not magenta-violet, and that exception is
deliberate.
HER EYES ARE COVERED BY THE GOLD BAND AND STAY COVERED. She is turned fully
toward his face, head slightly inclined, and the picture must read as her
attending to him closely — but nothing shows through the gold, and there are
no eyes to find behind it.
SO THE KINDNESS HAS TO LAND IN THE MOUTH AND THE TILT OF THE HEAD, and it
must land: GENUINE, WARM, UNFAKED CARE, from somebody who believes completely
that she is helping. Not sinister, not smirking, not cold, not falsely gentle,
and above all not blank — a covered face is an invitation to draw a mask, and
a mask is exactly wrong here. Somebody shown only her face should think they
were looking at a healer who loves her work. The horror is entirely in the
situation, and if she reads as a villain the plate has failed.
Her gold-and-black vestments are the only rich, ornate, expensive thing in a
room made of white tile, and that contrast is worth composing for.
FOUR SANDMEN stand along the wall in desert-gray, hoods up, EVENLY SPACED and
in IDENTICAL POSTURE — weight settled the same way, hands the same, heads at the
same angle, as though all four are listening to one slow song. They are doing
NOTHING. Not approaching, not watching intently, not reaching. Their flat,
even attention is the threat.
Wide, slightly high, taking in the table, the woman and all four figures.
White tile, white ceiling, desert-gray Sandman robes, and skin tones —
everything in the room is white, near-white or grey EXCEPT her, and her
gold is the only saturated colour in the plate. Her silver circuits are the
faintest thing in it.

blocks.v: He hadn't been tired. He'd found a door. And four days later a small Valari woman with frost-colored circuits had put her hand on his head in a white room and taken the door away, and been kind to him while she did it, and somebody, some office, some referral he had never requested, had sent him to her.
Cole knew who she was. Everybody in Haven City knew who she was, the way you know about lightning. You just never expect to find out you've been struck.

He looked out the window. The morning was coming up over the city, over the Tower standing gold against the haze, over the registration line already forming at the gate. Down below all of it, under the streets, there was a block full of people that god had forgotten, and a man with a book full of names, and at least one door that somebody thought was worth sending Sister Silence's people to close.
They'd taken it once and he'd gotten it back by accident, because a pencil didn't care what a god remembered.
Cole picked up the pencil. Under the old entry he wrote the date, and then:
*Second time. Same door. Same man. My name is in his book twice now. Three years ago somebody sent the gray hoods to take this out of my head. Find out who. Find out why the door matters that much.*

He tore the page out, folded it, and put it in his chest pocket, where he could feel it when he moved. Then he closed the notebook, finished his coffee, and went to work, because the city was full of broken things, and as of this morning he was the only man in it who knew that some of them were being broken on purpose.

image.caption: A pencil did not care what a god remembered.
image.depicts: Cole at his kitchen window as the morning comes up over Haven City — the Tower gold against the haze, the registration line already forming at the gate far below.
image.spoilerCheck: PASS. Closes the volume looking outward. The registration line is distant and anonymous; no climber is identifiable and the ceremony is four months away.
image.hardConstraints: The torn page is FOLDED and going into his chest pocket, or already in it — not open, not readable. The Tower is distant and small in frame; this is a man looking at a city, not a hero looking at a destination.
image.prompt:
{{STYLE}}
PALETTE MODE: PS-2 SUNSET EMBER, read as DAWN rather than dusk.
{{CHAR:COLE}}
ONE FIGURE. Cole at his kitchen window, seen from inside the room, mostly in
silhouette against the morning.
AFTER ELEVEN PLATES OF ENCLOSURE — a shaft, a gallery, a wall, a corridor, a
buried street, a windowless room — THIS IS THE FIRST OPEN HORIZON IN THE
VOLUME. Give it distance. That release is the point of the composition.
Through the window, Haven City in early morning haze: rooftops and blockwork in
the near ground, the city running back into the light, and THE TOWER standing
gold against the haze in the middle distance. THE TOWER IS SMALL IN FRAME and
far away. This is a man looking at a city he lives in, NOT a hero regarding a
destination — do not make it heroic and do not centre it on him.
At the foot of the Tower, just legible at that distance, a THIN DARK LINE of
people already forming at the gate. Anonymous, tiny, unresolved. Nobody in that
line is identifiable and nothing about it is dramatic.
Cole stands at the window with one hand at his chest pocket. THE TORN PAGE IS
FOLDED and is going into that pocket, or is already in it — a small folded
square of paper, closed, with nothing on it readable. His other hand holds a
finished cup of coffee.
His posture is not defiant, not resolved, not triumphant. It is the posture of
a man who has decided to go to work. THE LENS IS OFF.
Wide, level, from inside the kitchen and behind him, so the room is a dark frame
around a bright window and he is a dark shape inside it.
Burnt orange and amber sky with graphic cloud banding, warm ochre haze, deep
navy interior silhouettes, the Tower's gold the brightest small region in the
plate. The room around him is the darkest thing in the picture.
